newsitem.title: USA: Woman wanted Cosby seen as deadbeat dad.
newsitem.headline: Woman wanted Cosby seen as deadbeat dad.

text.p: A woman charged with trying to extort $40 million from Bill Cosby threatened to destroy his image as a perfect father by portraying him as a deadbeat dad, a prosecutor said Wednesday.

The accusation was made in an opening statement at the trial of Autumn Jackson, 22, who is accused of trying to ruin Cosby's reputation by going public with her claim to be the entertainer's illegitimate daughter and trying to sell her story to the Globe supermarket tabloid newspaper.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Paul Engelmeyer told a Manhattan federal court jury Jackson had wanted to attack Cosby's reputation as a family man and father and had drafted letters to CBS and Cosby's television sponsors including Eastman Kodak and Philip Morris Cos. that portrayed him as a "hypocrite" who did not deserve admiration and respect.

The "scathing" letters said Cosby had refused to pay her money and that she was forced to spend last Christmas eve sleeping in a box in a public park. But Engelmeyer said that in fact, Jackson and her fiance spent the evening in a hotel paid for with $3,000 Cosby had given Jackson for education.

"She would claim that despite his public image as a great dad, to her Bill Cosby had been a deadbeat dad," the prosecutor said. He said the letters were part of a get-rich-quick scheme orchestrated by Jackson and two accomplices in which they threatened to sell Jackson's story to the Globe unless Cosby paid them off.

Engelmeyer said evidence at trial will include a $25,000 contract with the Globe that was faxed to Cosby's lawyer with the threat Jan. 16. "They were driven by greed. They wanted to get rich quick ... The threat to Bill Cosby was simple ... your money or your reputation," he said.

Jackson's lawyer, Robert Baum, argued that there was no extortion and that his client was negotiating a settlement of what she saw as her "moral and legal" rights as Cosby's daughter. "This framed her intent in this case. It was not an intent to extort," Baum said.

He alleged that Cosby had been paying support money to Jackson and her mother for many years with the understanding they would never reveal that he was Jackson's father. Because of this, Jackson believed she could never be part of Cosby's life and attempted to reach a final settlement through negotiations with Cosby's lawyer in January, Baum said.
He said she placed an "opening bid on the table" of $40 million. "Autumn Jackson had nothing to hide. She was doing nothing unlawful in her mind," Baum said.

Cosby has admitted to having had an affair with Jackson's mother but has denied being her father. According to court papers, Jackson was one of many young people whose educational expenses Cosby paid for several years.

Actual paternity is not an issue in the trial. Jackson and the other defendants, Jose Medina, 51, and Boris Sabas, 42, are accused of conspiracy, extortion and violating a federal law that prohibits people from engaging in interstate commerce to commit certain offences. If convicted on all counts, they face possible prison terms of 12 years and fines of $750,000.
Lawyers said the three worked out of a motel room in Burbank, Calif., where they tried to put together a children's television show called "Down on the Farm." The programme never got off the ground.

The extortion plot came at a tragic time for the Cosby family. The entertainer's only son, Ennis, 27, was shot to death in California on Jan. 16, two days before Jackson was charged. Authorities have said the incidents are unrelated.
